Posted May 5, 2003
Analysis By Richard Cowan
Sir Francis Bacon said, " Truth can never be reached by just listening to the voice of an authority. "

As if to prove Bacon's point, the May 3rd issue of the British Medical Journal has an editorial, Comparing cannabis with tobacco.

The authors press release (see below) says, Cannabis smoking could be responsible for up to 30,000 deaths in the UK. That disturbing number is based on the assumption that tobacco and cannabis have comparable risks.

If their argument were accurate, what would be the public policy implications?

I would argue that from a public health perspective, this would be just one more reason to legalize cannabis. After all, the authors note that tobacco use has been falling, as a result of anti-smoking campaigns, while cannabis use has been rising, so prohibition is not working.

Moreover, the Dutch have a much lower rate of cannabis use than does the UK.
See
Canada Discovers The Netherlands As Senator Nolin Goes To Washington. What Bush/Ashcroft/Walters Really Fear: An Honest Debate On The Issues. We Are Winning!
and
Good News From Holland Is Even Better in Context. Large Majority of Dutch Parliament Favors Legalization of Cannabis. Most EU Countries Recognize Dutch Model Superior to DEAland's. We Are Winning!

Also, legalization would make it easier to reduce the risks associated with smoking, by encouraging vaporization instead of burning, and would also eliminate other risks inherent in contraband products, such as contamination, etc.
See
NORML -MAPS Study Shows Vaporizers Reduce Toxins in Marijuana Smoke.

In short, the arguments for the legalization of cannabis are not based on the assumption that cannabis is harmless. Nothing is harmless for everyone, at all doses and under all circumstances; consequently, harmlessness cannot be a prerequisite for anything being legal.
See
Marijuana Isn't Harmless. Okay, But Why Isn't Sold Over the Counter? Or Would You Ban Something That Causes 300,000 ER Visits Every Year, And Kills A Child Every Month? (Trick Question)

Rather, the arguments against cannabis prohibition are based on the idea that the laws are actually counterproductive.
See
Calling All Quacks: The Therapeutic Police State and the Politicization of Medicine. Doctors Cannot Study The Violence of Cannabis Prohibition. Because They Are The Disease, Not The Cure.

On the other hand, if the arguments by these authorities really were found to be dishonest and incompetent, what would be the public policy implications?

To put the matter very bluntly, what should we make of a situation in which the journal of the British Medical Association would print something with numerous errors of fact and logic?

The BMJ web site says. The BMJ aims to publish rigorous, accessible and entertaining material that will help doctors and medical students in their daily practice, lifelong learning and career development. In addition, it seeks to be at the forefront of the international debate on health We can publish only about 9% of more than 6000 articles that we receive each year, but we aim to give quick decisions
(emphasis added)

In their own words, the BMJ seeks to be at the forefront of the international debate on health. Moreover, they reject roughly 90% of all submissions, so it is only appropriate to hold the BMJ to very high standards and to be very concerned when so prestigious a journal falls far short of its own standards.

So which is the case? Is cannabis as dangerous as tobacco or is the BMJ an intellectual scandal? It really has to be one way or the other. Sadly, this is not the first time that I have had to raise this question.
See
The British Medical Journal Continues Its Mediocre Coverage of the Cannabis Issues and The Media Continue Their Wretched Journalism. Missing Essential Point That A Cannabinoid Is Not Whole Cannabis

Now let's begin with the authors press release, and notice the numerous qualifiers, if, assuming, could be, would be, potential effects, associated with, still little evidence,difficulties involved in gathering the data, despite the lack of evidence at the moment

I have highlighted some problems, but I will comment only on the editorial itself.

Subject: marijuana study - press release
Embargoed for release: 1-May-2003 18:00 Eastern US Time
Imperial College of Science, Technology and Medicine

Cannabis more damaging to health than previously thought claim doctors

Cannabis smoking could be responsible for up to 30,000 deaths in the UK, estimate doctors from Imperial College London and St Mary's Hospital.

Their editorial published in today's British Medical Journal, argues that cannabis could be a major contributor to deaths in the UK. The researchers calculate that if 120,000 deaths are caused among 13 million smokers, the corresponding figure among 3.2 million cannabis smokers would be 30,000, assuming that their health effects are the same.

Professor John Henry from Imperial College London, and one of the authors, comments: " Even if the number of deaths attributable to cannabis smoking turned out to be a fraction of the 30,000 we believe could be possible, cannabis smoking would still be described as a major health hazard. If we also add in the likely mental health burden to that of medical illnesses and premature death, the potential effects of cannabis cannot be ignored. "

Although it has been well documented that cannabis use is associated with an increased incidence of mental disorders, it could have a major effect on the respiratory system.

Dr William Oldfield from St Mary's Hospital, and one of the editorial's authors, adds: " Cannabis and nicotine cigarettes have a very different mode of inhalation, with cannabis smokers taking a two thirds larger puff volume, a third larger inhalation, and holding the smoke down four times as long. These could all contribute to illnesses of the heart and respiratory system, particularly as the chemicals in cannabis smoke are retained to a much higher degree. "

The level of active ingredient in cannabis, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) has increased from around 0.5 per cent twenty years ago to almost 5 per cent today. THC also has marked effects on the heart and blood vessels, and sudden deaths have been attributed to cannabis smoking.

Dr Onn Min Kon from St Mary's Hospital, and one of the editorial's authors, adds: " At present there is still little evidence of cardiopulmonary harm from cannabis, and there are difficulties involved in gathering the data necessary. Despite the lack of evidence at the moment, this is still no reason for people to assume that cannabis is harmless, and cannabis users need to be fully aware of the risks. "

Despite the fact that the number of tobacco smokers has been steadily decreasing due to public awareness of the harm caused, the numbers of cannabis smokers is increasing. Between 1999 and 2001, the number of 14 to 15 year olds who had tried cannabis rose from 19% to 29% in boys, and 18% to 25% in girls.

-end-

Now, The BMJ editorial:

Can we compare cannabis with tobacco?

There are now 13 million tobacco smokers in Britain. This number has been steadily decreasing due to public awareness of the harm caused by tobacco smoking. At the same time, the number of cannabis smokers is increasing. Between 1999 and 2001, the number of 14 to 15-year olds who had tried cannabis rose from 19% to 29% in boys and from 18% to 25% in girls,and a Home Office document estimates that there are 3.2 million cannabis smokers in Britain.1,2
(MarijuanaNews note: The first problem. The number of cannabis smokers is not directly comparable with the number of tobacco smokers because of the very different consumption patterns. Tobacco is highly addictive and most smokers are frequent daily users, while most cannabis smokers are infrequent users. So it is not realistic to extrapolate from one to the other.)

However, the harmful effects of cannabis smoking are widely known and have recently been highlighted.3,4(MarijuanaNews note: No. They are saying that something is widely known when it has just been asserted in two articles which have serious flaws.

Note 3 is the recent British Lung Foundation report, which I have analysed previously. It is a truly wretched piece of work, and is the basis for most of the BMJ editorial.
See
British Lung Foundation Cons Media. Blaming Cannabis for Problems Caused By Prohibition. Tripping Over the Party Line. The Media Fell For It, As Usual, But UK Anti-Tobacco Group Does Not.

Note 4 is Cannabis and mental health. BMJ 2002;325:1183-4 which has been strongly criticised, in part because there has been no increase in the incidence of schizophrenia, even though cannabis use has increased.
Also see
Classic Reefer Madness At London Times: " Woman who killed father 'driven mad by cannabis.' " Quacks and Hacks and Schizophrenia. Is It Paranoid to Distrust Politicized Science?

While the active ingredients of the cannabis plant differ from those of the tobacco plant, each produces about 4000 chemicals when smoked, and they are largely identical. Although cannabis cigarettes are smoked less frequently than nicotine cigarettes, their mode of inhalation is very different. Compared with tobacco smoking, cannabis smoking involves a two-thirds larger puff volume, a one-third larger inhaled volume, a four-fold longer breath hold time and a five-fold increase in blood carboxyhaemoglobin.5
(MarijuanaNews note: As I said in my critique of the BLF article, they are blaming cannabis for the way that it is smoked, which is an artefact of prohibition. It is not necessary to hold one's breath when smoking cannabis, but the high cost of contraband has encouraged this unfortunate custom.

They also completely ignore vaporization, and other ways of consuming it that do not involve burning it.)

The products of combustion from cannabis are thus retained to a much higher degree. How is this likely to translate into adverse effects on health? We already know that regular cannabis use is associated with an increased incidence of mental illnesses, most notably schizophrenia and depression,4 but it is also worth examining its potential to cause other illnesses, especially those of the heart and respiratory system. (MarijuanaNews note: Again, they are treating as fact these points that are really just assertions. To be associated with is not at all the same thing as causation.)

At present, there is an understandable dearth of epidemiological evidence of cardiopulmonary harm from cannabis, because its use is relatively new and its potency is changing.
(MarijuanaNews note: Cannabis has been widely used in the UK for decades, so it is not relatively new. Tobacco cigarettes did not become widely used until well into the 20th century, just a few decades before cannabis became popular. As for potency)

The amount of the main active constituent, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) in cannabis has increased from about 0.5% 20 years ago to nearer 5% at present in Britain, while Nederweed (the variety smoked in the Netherlands) has an average of 10-11% THC.
(MarijuanaNews note: A real howler!

If the editors of the BMJ knew anything about cannabis, or did any fact checking, that last paragraph should have put this article in the trash. Twenty years ago, almost all of the cannabis consumed in the UK was hashish, the average potency of which has always necessarily been well above the cannabis from which it is concentrated, so there is no data to support the idea that hashish in the UK averaged just 0.5% THC.

It was just this year that whole cannabis came to represent half of the UK market.
See
 International Update: Preview of NORML Conference Report On Developments In Cannabis Policies Around the World By Richard Cowan.

Twenty years ago in DEAland the average THC content of seized marijuana, almost none being hashish, was around 3%.

As for Nederweed - or more properly Nederwiet - that is not the variety smoked in the Netherlands, but rather just any cannabis that is grown there. It is not inherently any different from the cannabis grown in the UK or Canada or DEAland from the same seeds, using the growing same methods. The average Dutch grower probably has more experience than the average UK grower, but that is the only difference. In short, these quacks don't know what they are talking about.)
See
Potent Pot Myth Undermined By Report From The Ultimate Authority. Cited By Swedish Prohibitionist Who Don't Seem To Understand. As Usual.

At the same time, there has been little study of any concomitant change in tar content. Case-control studies are difficult to perform, since cannabis cigarettes do not come in standard sizes, making dose-response relationships difficult to establish. Furthermore, the majority of cannabis users also smoke tobacco, making it difficult to dissect out individual risks. As with tobacco, there will be a latent period between the onset of smoking and the development of lung damage, cardiovascular disease or malignant change.

Tobacco smoking is responsible for 120,000 excess deaths each year in Britain, 46,000 from cancers, 34,000 from chronic respiratory disorders and 40,000 from diseases of the heart and circulation.However, there are indications that smoked cannabis may cause similar effects to tobacco smoking, with many of them appearing at a younger age.

Cannabis smoking causes chronic bronchitis, emphysema and other lung disorders, which were recently summarised in a review released by the British Lung Foundation.3
(MarijuanaNews note: This is another howler that should get them barred from any serious journal. Regarding emphysema, the BLF article says, The evidence concerning a possible link between cannabis smoking and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) has not yet been conclusively established. A number of studies indicate a causal relationship between the two whereas others contradict these findings.

However, even the BLF article was playing games with the facts. Actually, the BLF's authority and everyone else's on the subject is Donald Tashkin. The BLF article's footnote #50, Tashkin, DP, Simmons, MS, Sherrill, D, et al, 1997, says, Heavy habitual marijuana smoking does not cause an accelerated decline in FEV1 with age: a longitudinal study, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 155, 141-148

[FEV1 is the amount of air that can be forcefully exhaled in the first second from a full inhalation.] The leading authority that they cite throughout has concluded that basic respiratory function is not damaged by even heavy marijuana smoking. That would seem to undermine the premise of the article. Moreover, this study is much later than the ones that say that it might cause such damage.
From the abstract:
To assess the possible role of daily smoking of marijuana in the development of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), we evaluatedthe effect of habitual use of marijuana with or without tobacco on theage-related change in lung function (measured as FEV1) in comparison withthe effect of nonsmoking and regular tobacco smoking. A convenience sampleof 394 healthy young Caucasian adults (68% men; age: 33 +/- 6 yr; mean +/-SD) including, at study entry, 131 heavy, habitual smokers of marijuanaalone, 112 smokers of marijuana plus tobacco, 65 regular smokers of tobaccoalone, and 86 nonsmokers of either substance were recruited from thegreater Los Angeles community. FEV1 was measured in all 394 participants atstudy entry and in 255 subjects (65 %) on up to six additional occasions atintervals of > or = 1 yr (1.7 +/- 1.1 yr) over a period of 8 yr.Random-effects models were used to estimate mean rates of decline in FEV1and to compare these rates between smoking groups. Although men showed asignificant effect of tobacco on FEV1 decline (p < 0.05), in neither mennor women was marijuana smoking associated with greater declines in FEV1than was nonsmoking, nor was an additive effect of marijuana and tobacconoted, or a significant relationship found between the number of marijuana cigarettes smoked per day and the rate of decline in FEV1. We conclude thatregular tobacco, but not marijuana, smoking is associated with greaterannual rates of decline in lung function than is nonsmoking. These findingsdo not support an association between regular marijuana smoking and chronicCOPD but do not exclude the possibility of other adverse respiratoryeffects.
Also see
Claim Three: " Smoking Marijuana Can Lead To Abnormal Functioning Of Lung Tissue. " New Scientist Special Report

A striking feature of cannabis smoking is that it is associated with bullous lung disease in young people.6 Inflammatory lung changes, chronic cough and chest infections are similar to those in cigarette smokers, but may also be commoner in younger people.7-9 Premalignant changes are demonstrable in the pulmonary epithelium, and there are reports of lung, tongue and other carcinomata in cannabis smokers.
See
Johns Hopkins Study Finds No Link Between Marijuana Use and Head, Neck, or Lung Cancer. There Was Also No Link Between This Study and Media Coverage.
and
What If Marijuana Could Cure Cancer? One More Reason Marijuana Prohibition Is Murder.

THC has cardiovascular effects, and sudden deaths have been attributed to cannabis smoking.10 Myocardial infarction is 4.2 times more likely to occur within an hour of smoking cannabis.11
See
Marijuana and " Heart Attack " Report Tells Us More About Media And Politicized Medicine Than About Marijuana. -- 2 Articles
(MarijuanaNews note: It is interesting that they spend so much time on the supposed risks posed by THC, but ignore the risks posed by nicotine.

As I reported in British Lung Foundation Cons Media. Blaming Cannabis for Problems Caused By Prohibition. Tripping Over the Party Line. The Media Fell For It, As Usual, But UK Anti-Tobacco Group Does Not., two researchers at The Scripps Research Institute announced last year that they had discovered that a chemical called nornicotine which is naturally present in tobacco and is also produced as a metabolite of nicotine may contribute to the pathology of diabetes, cancer, aging, and Alzheimer's disease.

Nornicotine also reacts with commonly prescribed steroids, like cortisone and prednisone, potentially making them more toxic or compromising their effectiveness and safety.

The article appears in the October 28, 2002 online edition of the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, but that apparently was not of any interest to the BLF, since there is no nornicotine in cannabis.

Also, Nature Medicine(July 2001 Volume 7 Number 7 pp 833 839) reported that nicotine on its own can cause cancer. Amazingly, the report says that nicotine had been widely seen as just being the drug that kept smokers addicted to tobacco, but otherwise was relatively harmless. That is very odd given that nicotine is highly toxic and acts as a vasoconstrictor.

The article says that nicotine at a concentration similar to that in the blood of tobacco smokers promoted cancerous tumor growth and narrowed arteries in mice, and accelerated growth of cancer tumors and fatty deposits on artery walls.)

However, despite these alarming facts, there is no evidence at present on whether cannabis smoking contributes to the progression of coronary artery disease as cigarette smoking does. More studies of the cardiovascular and pulmonary effects of cannabis are urgently needed.

It may be argued that the extrapolation from small numbers of individual studies to potential large scale effects is scaremongering. For example, one could calculate that if cigarettes cause an annual excess of 120,000 deaths among 13 million smokers, the corresponding figure for deaths among 3.2 million cannabis smokers would be 30,000, assuming equality of effect. Even if the number of deaths attributable to cannabis turned out to be a fraction of that figure, cannabis smoking would still be described as a major public health hazard.
See
Meanwhile UK Painkillers Kill 2,000 Per Year. But They Are Sold Over-the-Counter So They Must Be Safe!

However, when the likely mental health burden is added to the potential for morbidity and premature death from cardiopulmonary disease, these signals cannot be ignored. A recent comment said, Prevention and cessation are the two principal strategies in the battle against tobacco. ".12 At present, there is no battle against cannabis and no clear public health message.
(MarijuanaNews note: No battle against cannabis. "??? There have been tens of thousands of arrests every year in the UK for cannabis possession for decades. Even sick and dying people have been prosecuted and jailed for growing it.

What do these quacks want, a reefer madness campaign like that in DEAland, or perhaps the death penalty?)
See
Wide Range Of Consequences For People Caught with Cannabis in UK.
and
UK Government Cynicism: Change in Cannabis Laws to Benefit Son of " Justice " Minister, But Not the Sick and Dying.
and
The Complete Intellectual and Moral Bankruptcy of UK Cannabis Policies. 3 Articles.

John A Henry FRCP
Professor, Academic Department of Accident and Emergency Medicine, Imperial College School of Medicine, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY.

William LG Oldfield MRCP
Specialist Registrar, Department of Respiratory Medicine, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY.

Onn Min Kon FRCP
Consultant, Department of Respiratory Medicine, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY.
(Text 728 words)

(MarijuanaNews note: I strongly urge that you see the Rapid responses to the article on the BMJ web site. They are devastating.

And, one last point. Quacks have consequences.

The ignorance of doctors causes direct harm to the sick and dying. The following item was on the London Timesweb site last week:

From The London Times
April 29, 2003

In the professional press

WHAT are Britain's health professionals worrying about this week? Not Sars, that's for sure

Community Care discusses the case of an agency carer who refuses to work for Rosa, a multiple sclerosis sufferer who smokes, and grows, cannabis to ease her pain. Describing the patient as a drug addict, the carer has demanded that social services call in the police.
(emphasis added)

What to do? She should still be given care, the panel agrees. But maybe the carer's health could be protected by using a mask to prevent smoke inhalation, suggests James Lampert, a senior occupational therapist. Perhaps Rosa could be informed about the serious nature of both smoking and cultivating cannabis, says Sheila Hart, a health and disability team manager. But Simon Heng, a disabled service user, says: If people are convinced that they can alleviate their own distress by taking cannabis, who can blame them for stretching the letter of the law?)
